theorem.raw:
\label{thm:distributed-single-sensor-selection}
For every $\alpha \in [1, \infty)$ there is a protocol for the
  multiarmed bandit problem such that the worst case expected regret
  is
$\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\textsf{OPT} \ensuremath{n} \log \ensuremath{n}} + \textsf{OPT} e^{-\alpha})$, where
  $\textsf{OPT}$ is the total reward of the best action, and in each round at most 
$\alpha\paren{1 + (e-1)/\alpha}$ sensors communicate with the server and at most 
$2\alpha\paren{1 + (e-1)/\alpha}$ messages are exchanged in
expectation.
Moreover, there is a protocol with worst case expected regret
$\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\textsf{OPT} \ensuremath{n} \log \ensuremath{n}})$ and in each round 
only $\mathcal{O}(\log \ensuremath{n})$ sensors  communicate with the server and 
$\mathcal{O}(\log \ensuremath{n})$ messages are exchanged with high probability.

Moreover, there is a protocol with worst case expected regret O(sqrtOPT ensuremathn log ensuremathn) and in each round only O(log ensuremathn) sensors communicate with the server and O(log ensuremathn) messages are exchanged with high probability.

theorem.raw:
\label{thm:dog-performance}
The {\algofont{DOG}}\xspace algorithm selects, at each round $t$ a set
$S_{t}\subseteqV$ of $k$ sensors such that
\[
\frac{1}{T}\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}f_{t}(S_{t})\right]\geq
\frac{1-\frac{1}{e}}{T}\max_{|S|\leq k} \sum_{t=1}^{T} f_{t}(S) -
O\left(k\sqrt{\frac{n\log n}{T}}\right).
\]
In expectation, only $\mathcal{O}(k)$ messages are exchanged each round.

\label{thm:better-lazydog}

  The variant of \algofont{lazyDOG}\xspace that runs the \LimitProtocol$(\alpha)$ with lazy
  renormalization for $\ensuremath{k}' := \ceil{\ensuremath{k}/(1 - e^{-\alpha})}$ stages, but
  does not rerun it if nothing is selected in a given stage, has

\algofont{lazyDOG}\xspace is at most

proof.raw:
To prove the regret bounds, note that in every round the distribution over sensor
selections in the variant of {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace we describe 
(that uses the distributed multinomial sampling scheme and repeatedly reruns the protocol in
order to always select some sensor in each round) is precisely the
same as the original {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace.  Thus the regret bounds for
{\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace~\cite{auer02} carry over unchanged.
We next bound the number of broadcasts.  Fix a round, and let $S$ set
of sensors that activate in that round.  The total number of broadcasts is
then $|S|+2$; using their calibrated clocks, each sensor (re)samples  
$X_{\ensuremath{v}} \sim \Poisson{\alpha p_{\ensuremath{v}} }$ and activates if
$X_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1$.  If no sensors activate before a specified
timeout period, the default behavior is to rerun the sampling step.
Eventually $|S| \ge 1$ sensors activate in the same period.  A
distinguished sensor in $S$ then determines the selected sensor $\ensuremath{v}$,
broadcasts $\ensuremath{\operatorname{id}}(\ensuremath{v})$, and $\ensuremath{v}$ broadcasts its observed reward.
We prove $\E{|S|} \le \alpha / (1 - e^{-\alpha})$ in
Proposition~\ref{prop:broadcast-activations}.  When $\alpha = 1$, this
gives us the claimed bound on the number of broadcasts.

Thus the regret bounds for algofontEXP3xspace carry over unchanged. We next bound the number of broadcasts. Fix a round, and let S set of sensors that activate in that round. The total number of broadcasts is then |S|+2; using their calibrated clocks, each sensor (re)samples X_ensuremathv sim Poissonalpha p_ensuremathv and activates if X_ensuremathv ge 1. We prove E|S| le alpha / (1 - e^-alpha) in Proposition~. When alpha = 1, this gives us the claimed bound on the number of broadcasts.

proof.raw:
Let $X_{\ensuremath{v}} \sim \Bernoulli{\alpha \cdot p_{\ensuremath{v}}}$ be the indicator random
variable for the activation of $\ensuremath{v}$, and let $X := \sum_{\ensuremath{v}}
X_{\ensuremath{v}}$.  The expected number of sensor activations is then
\[
\E{X \ |\ X \ge 1} = \E{X}/\prob{X \ge 1} \mbox{.}
\]
In the limit as $\max_{\ensuremath{v}} p_{\ensuremath{v}}$ tends to zero, $X$
converges to a Poisson random variable with mean $\alpha$.
In this case, $\frac{\E{X}}{\prob{X \ge 1}} = \alpha / (1 - e^{-\alpha})$
To see that this is an upper bound, consider an arbitrary distribution
$p$ on the sensors, and fix some $\ensuremath{v}$ with $x := p_{\ensuremath{v}} > 0$.
We claim that replacing $\ensuremath{v}$ with two sensors $\ensuremath{v}_1$ and
$\ensuremath{v}_2$ with positive probability mass $x_1$ and
$x_2$ with $x = x_1+x_2$ can only serve to increase the expected number of
sensor activations, because $\E{X}$ is unchanged, and $\prob{X \ge 1}$
decreases.  The latter is true essentially because 
$\prob{\exists i \in \set{1,2}: \ensuremath{v}_i \text{ activates}} = 1 -
(1-x_1)(1-x_2) = x - x_1x_2 < x$.  To complete the proof, notice that 
repeating this process with $\ensuremath{v} = \argmax (p_{\ensuremath{v}})$ and $x_i = x/2$ ensures $X$
converges to a Poisson variable with mean $\alpha$, while only
increasing $\E{X \ |\ X \ge 1}$.

proof.raw:
Lazy renormalization
selects each sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ with probability
$(1-e^{-\alpha})p_{\ensuremath{v}}$, because of the way the random bits
$r_{\ensuremath{v}}$ are shared in order to implement a coupled distribution for
sensor activation and selection.
Note that it would be sufficient to run the \LimitProtocol on the correct (possibly
oversampled) probabilities, $\alpha p_{\ensuremath{v}}$, 
since then~\propref{thm:sampling} ensures that each $\ensuremath{v}$
is selected with probability $(1 - e^{-\alpha}) p_{\ensuremath{v}}$.
The difficulty is that $\ensuremath{v}$ does not have access to the correct
normalizer $Z(t)$, but only its estimate (lower bound) for it,
$Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$.
To overcome this difficulty, we define a joint probability
distribution over two random variables $(X_{\ensuremath{v}},
Y_{\ensuremath{v}})$, where 
\[
X_{\ensuremath{v}}  = X_{\ensuremath{v}}(R) := \left\{ 
\begin{array}{ll} 
1 & \text{if $R \ge 1 - \alpha \cdot\rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t))$} \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{array}  \right.
\]
\[
Y_{\ensuremath{v}} = Y_{\ensuremath{v}}(R) := \min \set{b \ :\ \sum_{a=0}^b \frac{e^{-\lambda}
    \lambda^{a}}{a!} \ge R }
\]
and $\lambda := \alpha \cdot \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z(t))$, and $R$ is
sampled uniformly at random from $[0,1]$.
Now, note that $Y_{\ensuremath{v}}$ is distributed as $\Poisson{\lambda}$.
Also note that $Y_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1$ implies $X_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1$,
because $Y_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1$ implies $R \ge e^{-\lambda}$ and 
\[
 e^{-\lambda}  \ge 1 - \lambda \ge 1 - \alpha \cdot \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t))
\]
since $1 + x \le e^x$ for all $x \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$, and $\rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t),
Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)) \ge \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z(t))$ due to fact
that $Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) \le Z(t)$.
It follows that we can use the event $X_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1$ as a
conservative indicator that $\ensuremath{v}$ should activate.
In this case, it will send its sampled value for $R$, namely
$r_{\ensuremath{v}}$, and its weight $w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$ to the server.  
The server knows $Z(t)$, and then can
use $r_{\ensuremath{v}}$ and $w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$ to compute
$Y_{\ensuremath{v}}(r_{\ensuremath{v}})$, 
the sample from $\Poisson{\lambda}$ that $\ensuremath{v}$ would have
drawn had it known $Z(t)$.  The resulting distribution on selected
sensors is thus exactly the same as in the \LimitProtocol without lazy
renormalization.
Invoking~\propref{thm:sampling} thus completes the proof.

proof.raw:
Fix $\ensuremath{v}$, and let $p(t) := p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$, $q(t) := q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$.
We begin by bounding $\prob{q(t) \ge \lambda p(t)}$ for $\lambda \ge
1$.  Let $t_0$ be the most recent round in which $q(t_0) = p(t_0)$.
We assume $q(0) = p(0)$, so $t_0$ exists.
Then $q(t) = p(t_0) \ge \lambda p(t)$  implies $p(t_0)/p(t)
\ge \lambda$.  By assumption $p(t')/p(t'+1) \le (1+\hat{\epsilon})$
for all $t'$, so $p(t_0)/p(t) \le (1+\hat{\epsilon})^{t-t_0}$.
Thus $\lambda \le (1+\hat{\epsilon})^{t-t_0}$ and 
$t-t_0 \ge \ln(\lambda)/ \ln (1+\hat{\epsilon})$. 
Define $t(\lambda) := \ln(\lambda)/ \ln (1+\hat{\epsilon})$.


By definition of $t_0$, there were no activations under lazy renormalization in rounds $t_0$
through $t-1$ inclusive, which occurs with probability 
$\prod_{t' = t_0}^{t-1} (1-\alpha q(t'))$ $=$ $(1-\alpha
q(t))^{t-t_{0}} $ $\le$ $(1-\alpha q(t))^{\ceil{t(\lambda)}}$, where $\alpha$ is the
oversampling parameter in the protocol.  


We now bound $\Econd{q(t)/p(t)}{q(t)}$.
Recall that $\E{X} = \int_{x = 0}^{\infty} \prob{X \ge x}dx$ for any non-negative
random variable $X$.  It will also be convenient to define 
$\ensuremath{\omega} := \ln(1/(1 - \alpha q(t))) / \ln(1+\hat{\epsilon})$ and assume for now
that $\ensuremath{\omega} > 1$.
Conditioning on $q(t)$, we see that 
\[
\begin{array}{lcl}
 \vspace{2mm}
\Econd{q(t)/p(t)}{q(t)} & = & \int_{\lambda = 0}^{\infty} \prob{q(t) \ge
  \lambda p(t)}d\lambda \\ 
 \vspace{2mm}
  & = & 1 + \int_{\lambda = 1}^{\infty} \prob{q(t) \ge
  \lambda p(t)}d\lambda \\ 
\vspace{2mm}
 & \le & 1 + \int_{\lambda = 1}^{\infty} (1-\alpha q(t))^{t(\lambda)}d\lambda\\
 \vspace{2mm}
 & = & 1 + \int_{\lambda = 1}^{\infty}
\lambda^{\ln(1-\alpha q(t))/\ln(1+\hat{\epsilon}) }d\lambda \\
 \vspace{2mm}
 & = & 1 + \int_{\lambda = 1}^{\infty} \lambda^{-\ensuremath{\omega}}d\lambda \\ 
 \vspace{2mm}
 & = & 1 + \frac{1}{\ensuremath{\omega} - 1}


\end{array}
\]
Using $\ln\paren{\frac{1}{1-x}} \ge x$ for all $x < 1$ and 
$\ln(1+x) \le x$ for all $x > -1$, we can show that 


$\ensuremath{\omega} \ge \alpha q(t)/\hat{\epsilon}$
so $1+\frac{1}{\ensuremath{\omega} - 1} \le \alpha
q(t)/(\alpha q(t) - \hat{\epsilon})$.
Thus, if $\alpha q(t) > \hat{\epsilon}$ then $\ensuremath{\omega} > 1$ and we
obtain 
$\Econd{q(t)/p(t)}{q(t)} \le  \alpha q(t)/(\alpha q(t) - \hat{\epsilon})$.


If $q(t) >> \hat{\epsilon}$, this gives a good bound.  If $q(t)$ is small, we
rely on the assumption that $p(t) \ge \epsilon$ for all $t$ to get a trivial
bound of $q(t)/p(t) \le q(t)/\epsilon$.
We thus conclude 
\begin{equation} \label{eqn:ratio-bound}
\Econd{q(t)/p(t)}{q(t)} \le \min \paren{\alpha q(t)/(\alpha q(t) - \hat{\epsilon}) ,\ q(t)/\epsilon}\mbox{.}
\end{equation}
Setting $q(t) = (\hat{\epsilon}/\alpha + \epsilon)$ to maximize this
quantity yields an unconditional bound of 


$\E{q(t)/p(t)} \le 1 + \hat{\epsilon}/\alpha\epsilon$.


To bound $\E{q(t)}$ in terms of $\E{p(t)}$, note that for all $q$
\begin{align*}
q/\Econd{p(t)}{q(t)=q} & \le \Econd{q(t)/p(t)}{q(t)=q}\\
                    & \le 1 + \hat{\epsilon}/\alpha\epsilon
\end{align*}
where the first line is by Jensen's inequality, and the second is by 
equation~\ref{eqn:ratio-bound}.
Thus $q \le \paren{1 +
  \hat{\epsilon}/\alpha\epsilon}\Econd{p(t)}{q(t)=q}$ for all $q$.
Taking the expectation with respect to $q$ then proves 
$\E{q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)} \le \paren{1 +
  \frac{\hat{\epsilon}}{\alpha\epsilon}} \E{p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)}$
as claimed.

proof.raw:
Fix a sensor $\ensuremath{v}$.  This sensor activates more frequently under
lazy renormalization only due to the fact that its estimate for 
$p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$, which we denote by $\bar{p}_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$, may be too high.
Suppose $\ensuremath{v}$ was last activated at time $\tau$.


The number of rounds before $\ensuremath{v}$ is activated again, under lazy
renormalization, is simply equal to the number of coin tosses of
a coin with bias $p_{\ensuremath{v}}(\tau+1)$ to come up heads, which is 
$\ensuremath{\mu_{\text{lazy}}} = 1/p_{\ensuremath{v}}(\tau+1)$ in expectation.
Under eager renormalization (where $p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$ is known exactly), 
the expected number of rounds $\ensuremath{\mu_{\text{eager}}}$ before $\ensuremath{v}$ is activated again is 
\[
\ensuremath{\mu_{\text{eager}}}(\tau) = \sum_{t = \tau+1}^{\infty} \paren{t-\tau}\paren{\prod_{t'=\tau+1}^{t-1}
  \paren{1 - p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t')}}p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) 
\]


It is not too hard to see that this expression is maximized by making
the $p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t')$ terms shrink as fast as possible.
That is, if we set 
$p_{\ensuremath{v}}(\tau+i) = p_{\ensuremath{v}}(\tau+1) \cdot \paren{1+\hat{\epsilon}}^{1-i}$, then 
the above expression provides an upper bound on $\ensuremath{\mu_{\text{eager}}}$.
Under these circumstances, the above expression satisfies the recurrence
\[
f(p) = 1 + (1-p)f(p/(1+\hat{\epsilon}))
\] 
where $f(p)$ is the value of $\ensuremath{\mu_{\text{eager}}}$ assuming $p_{\ensuremath{v}}(\tau+1) = p$.
Solving it yields 
\[
f(p) = \frac{1}{p(1+\hat{\epsilon}) - \hat{\epsilon}} \mbox{.}
\]
Simple algebra reveals that for all $c > 1$, if $p \ge \hat{\epsilon}c/(c-1)$ then 
$\ensuremath{\mu_{\text{eager}}} \le f(p) \le c/p = c \cdot \ensuremath{\mu_{\text{lazy}}}$.
On the other hand, if $p \le \hat{\epsilon}c/(c-1)$, we can use the
assumption that $p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) \ge \epsilon$ for all $t$ to show that 
$\ensuremath{\mu_{\text{eager}}} \le 1/\epsilon$, implying 
that $\ensuremath{\mu_{\text{eager}}}/\ensuremath{\mu_{\text{lazy}}} \le p/\epsilon \le \frac{\hat{\epsilon
    c}}{\epsilon (c-1)}$.  Balancing out the ratios of $c$ and
$\frac{\hat{\epsilon c}}{\epsilon (c-1)}$, we obtain a ratio of 
$c^* = 1 + \hat{\epsilon}/\epsilon$.

proof.raw:
The former equality is an easy observation.
To prove the latter equality, fix a round $t$ and a selected action
$\ensuremath{v}$.  Let 
$w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$ be the weight of $\ensuremath{v}$ in round $t$, and $W(t)$ be the
total weight of all actions in round $t$.
Let $\ensuremath{\pi}$ be the payoff to $\ensuremath{v}$ in round $t$.
Given the update rule 
$w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t+1) =
w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)\exp\paren{\frac{\gamma}{\ensuremath{n}}\frac{\ensuremath{\pi}(\ensuremath{v},t)}{p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)}}$,
only the probabilities of the other actions will be decreased.
It is not hard to see that they will be decreased by a multiplicative factor of at most 
$W(t)/W(t+1)$, no matter what the learning parameter $\gamma$ is.
By the update rule, 
\[
W(t+1) = W(t) +
w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)\paren{\exp\paren{\frac{\gamma}{\ensuremath{n}}
\frac{\ensuremath{\pi}}{p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)}}
    - 1}\mbox{.}
\]
Let $p := p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$ and $x :=
\frac{\gamma}{\ensuremath{n}}\ensuremath{\pi}$.  
Dividing the above equation by $W(t)$, we get 

\begin{align}
\frac{W(t+1)}{W(t)} & = 1 + p\paren{\exp\paren{x/p} - 1} \\
 & \le 1 + p\paren{x/p + (e-2)(x/p)^2}\\
 & \le 1 + x + (e-2)x^2/p
\end{align}

where in the second line we have used 
$e^x \le 1 + x + (e-2)x^2$ for $x \in [0,1]$.
Note $\ensuremath{\pi} \le 1$ implies $x \le \gamma/n \le p$, so 
$\frac{W(t+1)}{W(t)} \le 1 + (e-1)x \le 1 +
(e-1)\frac{\gamma}{\ensuremath{n}}$.
It follows that setting $\hat{\epsilon} =
(e-1)\frac{\gamma}{\ensuremath{n}}$ is sufficient to ensure 
$p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t+1) \ge p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)/(1+\hat{\epsilon})$ for all $t$.

proof.raw:
We prove in Lemma~\ref{lem:exp3conditions} that {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace satisfies
the conditions of Theorem~\ref{thm:lazy_renorm_ratio} 
with $\epsilon = \gamma/\ensuremath{n}$ and $\hat{\epsilon} =
(e-1)\frac{\gamma}{\ensuremath{n}}$.  Thus by Theorem~\ref{thm:lazy_renorm_ratio} 
\begin{align*}
\E{\sum_{\ensuremath{v}} q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)} & \le \paren{1 +
  (e-1)/\alpha}\E{\sum_{\ensuremath{v}} p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)}\\ & = \paren{1 +
  (e-1)/\alpha} 
\end{align*}
because $\sum_{\ensuremath{v}} p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) = 1$.
Each sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ activates with probability $\alpha q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$,
so the expected number of activations is 
\[
\E{\alpha \sum_{\ensuremath{v}} q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)} \le \alpha\paren{1 +
  (e-1)/\alpha}\mbox{.}
\]

That proves the claimed bounds in expectation.  To prove bounds with
high probability, note that a sensor activates with probability
$\alpha q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$ in round $t$, where   $q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$ is a
random variable.
Fix $t$.  Let $[\ensuremath{\mathcal{E}}]$ denote the indicator variable
for the event $\ensuremath{\mathcal{E}}$, i.e., $[\ensuremath{\mathcal{E}}] = 1$ if $\ensuremath{\mathcal{E}}$ occurs, and
$[\ensuremath{\mathcal{E}}] = 0$ otherwise.  Then we can write 
$[\ensuremath{v} \text{ activates in round }t] = [\alpha
q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) \ge R]$, where $R$ is sampled uniformly at random from
$[0,1]$ and $R$ is independent of $q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$.
Then if $f_R$ is the probability density functions of $R$ we can write 
\[
\begin{aligned}
   \prob{R \le \alpha q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)} & = \int_{r = 0}^1 \prob{\alpha
q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) \ge R \ |\  R = r} f_R(r) dr\\
  & = \int_{r = 0}^1 \prob{\alpha q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) \ge r} f_R(r) dr \\
& = \int_{r = 0}^1 \prob{\alpha q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) \ge r}dr \\
& = \E{ \alpha q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) }
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus the number of sensor activations is a sum of $|V|$ binary
random variables with cumulative mean 
$\mu := \sum_{\ensuremath{v}}  \E{ \alpha q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) }$.
We have already bounded this mean as $\mu \le \alpha + (e-1)$.
From here a simple application of a Chernoff-Hoeffding bound suffices
to prove that with high probability this sum is at most 
$\mathcal{O}(\alpha + \log n)$.  Let $A$ be the number of sensor activations.
Then, e.g., Theorem~$5$ of~\cite{CL06} 
immediately implies 
\[
\prob{A \ge \mu(1 + \delta)} \le \exp \paren{ - \frac{\delta^2
    \mu^2}{2 \mu + \frac{2\delta \mu}{3}}}
\]
For $\delta \ge 1$, this yields 
$\prob{A \ge \mu(1 + \delta)} \le \exp \paren{ -
  \frac{3\delta\mu}{8}}$.
Setting $\delta = 1 + \frac{8c\ln n}{3\mu}$ ensures this probability is
at most $n^{-c}$, hence 
$\prob{A \ge 2\mu + \frac{8}{3}c\ln n} \le n^{-c}$.
Noting that $\mu \le \alpha + (e-1)$ completes the high probability
bound on the number of activations.


As for the number of messages, note that each message involves a
sensor as sender or receiver, and by inspection the protocol only
involves two messages per activated node.

proof.raw:
Use the distributed {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace protocol with lazy
renormalization with $\alpha = \ln n$.  We have already established
that the probability of nothing being selected is $e^{-\alpha}$ or
$1/n$ in this case.  If nothing is selected, send out $n$ messages,
one to each sensor, to rerun the protocol.  The expected number of
messages sent to initiate additional runs of the protocol is 
$\sum_{x=1}^{\infty} nx/n^{x} = \paren{1 - 1/n}^{-2} = 1 + \mathcal{O}(1/n)$.
Let $X$ be the number of sensor activations.
As in the proof of
Proposition~\ref{prop:broadcast-activations}, if $Y$ is 
the expected number of sensor activations without rerunning the
protocol when nothing is selected, then 
$\E{X} = \E{Y}/\prob{Y \ge 1}$.  By
Theorem~\ref{thm:dexp3-performance} $\E{Y} \le  \alpha\paren{1 +
  (e-1)/\alpha}$.  Since $\prob{Y \ge 1} = 1 - e^{-\alpha}$, we 
conclude 
\[
\E{X} \le \ln n + (e-1) + \mathcal{O}\paren{\frac{\ln n}{n}}\mbox{.}
\]
The with-high-probability bounds on the number of sensor activations
are proved as in 
the proof of Corollary~\ref{cor:dexp3-performance}.

As for the number of messages, note that other than 
messages sent to initiate additional runs of the protocol, there are
only two messages per activated node.  Finally, the regret bounds for
distributed {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace are the same as standard {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace because by
design the two algorithms select sensors from exactly the same distribution in each
round.  Note that the distribution in any given round is a random
object depending on the algorithm's choices in the previous rounds,
however on each round the distribution on distributions is the same for both {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace
variants, as can be readily proved by induction on the round number.

The expected number of messages sent to initiate additional runs of the protocol is sum_x=1^infty nx/n^x = paren1 - 1/n^-2 = 1 + O(1/n). Let X be the number of sensor activations. As in the proof of Proposition~, if Y is the expected number of sensor activations without rerunning the protocol when nothing is selected, then EX = EY/probY ge 1. By Theorem~ EY le alphaparen1 + (e-1)/alpha. Since probY ge 1 = 1 - e^-alpha, we conclude \[ EX le ln n + (e-1) + Oparenfracln nnmbox. \] The with-high-probability bounds on the number of sensor activations are proved as in the proof of Corollary~. proof.raw:
It suffices to prove the analogous result in the offline case; the
``meta-actions'' analysis in~\cite{streeter07tr} can then be used to complete the proof.
So consider a set of elements $V$ and the ``faulty'' versions
$V'$.  Fix a monotone submodular $f:2^{V} \to [0,1]$ and
define $f'$ as above.  Run the offline greedy algorithm on $f'$ to try
to find the best set of $\ensuremath{k}' = \frac{\ensuremath{k}}{1-\delta}$ elements in $V'$.
Let $g'_i$ be the chosen element in stage $i$, and let $G'_i = \set{g'_j : 1
  \le j \le i}$.  Let $G_i$ denote the realization of $G'_i$ after
sampling, so that $G_i \subseteq \set{g : g' \in G'_i}$.
Let  $S^* = \argmax_{S \subseteq V, |S| \le \ensuremath{k}}(f(S))$.

We claim that for all $i$
\[
\Econd{f(G'_{i+1}) - f(G'_i)}{G_i} \ge \paren{1-\delta}
\frac{f(S^*) - f(G_i)}{\ensuremath{k}}
\]
because 
\begin{align*}
f(S^*) - f(G_i) & \le f(G_i \cup S^*) - f(G_i)\\
                & \le \sum_{\ensuremath{v} \in S^*} \paren{f(G_i + \ensuremath{v}) - f(G_i)}\\
                & \le \ensuremath{k} \cdot \max_{\ensuremath{v}} \paren{f(G_i + \ensuremath{v}) - f(G_i)}
\end{align*}
and $\max_{\ensuremath{v}'} \paren{\Econd{f(G'_i + \ensuremath{v}') - f(G'_i)}{G_i} }$ is at least equal to 
$(1-\delta)\max_{\ensuremath{v}} \paren{f(G_i + \ensuremath{v}) - f(G_i)}$.
Removing the conditioning on $G_i$ we get 
\[
\E{f(G'_{i+1}) - f(G'_i)} \ge \paren{1-\delta}\frac{f(S^*) -
  \E{f(G'_i)}}{\ensuremath{k}}
\]
Let $\Phi(i) = f(S^*) - \E{f(G'_{i})}$.  The previous equation implies 
$\Phi(i+1) \le \Phi(i)\paren{1 - \frac{1-\delta}{\ensuremath{k}}}$.

items.raw:
The Offline Sensor Selection Problem
\label{sec:offline-problem}
A standard offline sensor selection algorithm chooses a set of sensors
that maximizes a known sensing quality objective function $f({\mathcal{A}})$,
subject to some constraints,



e.g., on the number of activated sensors. One possible choice for the
sensing quality is based on prediction accuracy (we will discuss other
possible choices later on).  In many applications, measurements are
correlated across space, which allows us to make predictions at the
unobserved locations.  For example, prior work \cite{vldb04} has
considered the setting where a random variable ${\mathcal{X}}_{s}$ is associated
with every location $s\inV$, and a joint probability
distribution $P({\mathcal{X}}_{V})$ models the correlation between sensor
values.  Here, ${\mathcal{X}}_{V}=[{\mathcal{X}}_{1},\dots,{\mathcal{X}}_{\ensuremath{n}}]$ is
the random vector over all measurements.  If some measurements
${\mathcal{X}}_{{\mathcal{A}}}={\mathbf{x}}_{{\mathcal{A}}}$ are obtained at a subset of locations, then the
conditional distribution
$P({\mathcal{X}}_{V\setminus{\mathcal{A}}}\mid{\mathcal{X}}_{{\mathcal{A}}}={\mathbf{x}}_{{\mathcal{A}}})$ allows
predictions at the unobserved locations, e.g., by predicting
$\mathbb{E}[{\mathcal{X}}_{V\setminus{\mathcal{A}}}\mid{\mathcal{X}}_{{\mathcal{A}}}={\mathbf{x}}_{{\mathcal{A}}}]$.
Furthermore, this conditional distribution quantifies the
\emph{uncertainty} in the prediction: Intuitively, we would like to
select sensors that minimize the predictive uncertainty.  One way to
quantify the predictive uncertainty is the mean squared prediction
error,
$$\MSE({\mathcal{X}}_{V\setminus{\mathcal{A}}}\mid {\mathbf{x}}_{{\mathcal{A}}}) =
\frac{1}{\ensuremath{n}}\sum_{s\inV\setminus{\mathcal{A}}}
\mathbb{E}[({\mathcal{X}}_s-\mathbb{E}[{\mathcal{X}}_{s}\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{{\mathcal{A}}}])^{2}\mid
{\mathbf{x}}_{{\mathcal{A}}}].$$ In general, the measurements ${\mathbf{x}}_{{\mathcal{A}}}$ that sensors
${\mathcal{A}}$ will make is not known in advance.  Thus, we can base our
optimization on the \emph{expected mean squared prediction error},
$$\EMSE({\mathcal{A}}) = \int dp({\mathbf{x}}_{{\mathcal{A}}}) \MSE({\mathcal{X}}_{V\setminus{\mathcal{A}}}\mid {\mathbf{x}}_{{\mathcal{A}}}).$$
Equivalently, we can maximize the \emph{reduction} in mean squared prediction error,
$$f_{\EMSE}({\mathcal{A}}) = \EMSE(\emptyset)-\EMSE({\mathcal{A}}).$$ By definition,
$f_{\EMSE}(\emptyset)=0$, i.e., no sensors obtain no
utility. Furthermore, $f_{\EMSE}$ is monotonic: if
${\mathcal{A}}\subseteq{\mathcal{B}}\subseteqV$, then $f_{\EMSE}({\mathcal{A}})\leq
f_{\EMSE}({\mathcal{B}})$, i.e., adding more sensors always helps.  That means,
$f_{\EMSE}$ is maximized by the set of all sensors $V$.  However,
in practice, we would like to only select a small set of, e.g., at
most $k$ sensors due to bandwidth and power constraints:
$${\mathcal{A}}^*=\argmax_{{\mathcal{A}}}f_{\EMSE}({\mathcal{A}})\text{ s.t. }|{\mathcal{A}}|\leq k.$$
Unfortunately, this optimization problem is NP-hard, so we cannot
expect to efficiently find the optimal solution.  Fortunately, it can
be shown \cite{das07} that in many settings\footnote{For Gaussian
models and conditional suppressorfreeness \cite{das07}}, the function
$f_{\EMSE}$ satisfies an intuitive diminishing returns property called
submodularity.  A set function $f:2^{V}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$
is called \emph{submodular}

if, for all
${\mathcal{A}}\subseteq{\mathcal{B}}\subseteqV$ and $s\inV\setminus {\mathcal{B}}$ it
holds that $f({\mathcal{A}}\cup\{s\})-f({\mathcal{A}})\geq f({\mathcal{B}}\cup\{s\})-f({\mathcal{B}})$. Many
other natural objective functions for sensor selection satisfy
submodularity as well \cite{krause07nearoptimal}.  For example, the
\emph{sensing region} model where $\ensuremath{f}_{REG}({\mathcal{A}})$ is the total area
covered by all sensors ${\mathcal{A}}$ is submodular.  The \emph{detection}
model where $\ensuremath{f}_{DET}({\mathcal{A}})$ counts the expected number of targets
detected by sensors ${\mathcal{A}}$ is submodular as well.

A fundamental result of Nemhauser et al.~\cite{nemhauser78} is that
for monotone submodular functions, a simple greedy algorithm, which
starts with the empty set ${\mathcal{A}}_{0}=\emptyset$ and iteratively adds the
element $$s_{k}=\argmax_{s\inV\setminus {\mathcal{A}}_{k-1}}
f({\mathcal{A}}_{k-1}\cup\{s\});\ \ {\mathcal{A}}_{k}={\mathcal{A}}_{k-1}\cup\{s_{k}\}$$ which maximally improves the utility obtains a
near-optimal solution: For the set ${\mathcal{A}}_{k}$ it holds that
$$f({\mathcal{A}}_{k})\geq (1-1/e)\max_{|{\mathcal{A}}|\leq k}f({\mathcal{A}}),$$ i.e., the greedy
solution obtains at least a constant fraction of $(1-1/e)\approx 63\%$
of the optimal value.

\looseness -1 One fundamental problem with this offline approach is that it requires the function $f$ to be specified in advance, i.e., before running the greedy algorithm.  For the function $f_{\EMSE}$, this means that the probabilistic model $P({\mathcal{X}}_{V})$ needs to be known in advance.  While for some applications some prior data, e.g., from pilot deployments, may be accessible, very often no such prior data is available.  This leads to a ``chicken-and-egg'' problem, where sensors need to be activated to collect data in order to learn a model, but also the model is required to inform the sensor selection.  This is akin to the ``exploration--exploitation tradeoff'' in reinforcement learning \cite{auer02}, where an agent needs to decide whether to explore and gather information about effectiveness of an action, or to exploit, i.e., choose actions known to be effective. In the following, we devise an online monitoring scheme based on this analogy.

A fundamental result of Nemhauser et al. is that for monotone submodular functions, a simple greedy algorithm, which starts with the empty set A_0=emptyset and iteratively adds the element s_k=argmax_sinVsetminus A_k-1 f(A_k-1cup\s\);\ \ A_k=A_k-1cup\s_k\ which maximally improves the utility obtains a near-optimal solution: For the set A_k it holds that f(A_k)geq (1-1/e)max_|A|leq kf(A), i.e., the greedy solution obtains at least a constant fraction of (1-1/e)approx 63\% of the optimal value. looseness -1 One fundamental problem with this offline approach is that it requires the function f to be specified in advance, i.e., before running the greedy algorithm. For the function f_EMSE, this means that the probabilistic model P(X_V) needs to be known in advance. While for some applications some prior data, e.g., from pilot deployments, may be accessible, very often no such prior data is available. This leads to a ``chicken-and-egg'' problem, where sensors need to be activated to collect data in order to learn a model, but also the model is required to inform the sensor selection. This is akin to the ``exploration--exploitation tradeoff'' in reinforcement learning , where an agent needs to decide whether to explore and gather information about effectiveness of an action, or to exploit, i.e., choose actions known to be effective. In the following, we devise an online monitoring scheme based on this analogy.

items.raw:
The Online Sensor Selection Problem
\label{sec:online-problem}






We now consider the more challenging problem where the objective
function is not specified in advance, and needs to be learned during
the monitoring task.  We assume that we intend to monitor the
environment for a number $T$ of time steps (rounds).  In each round
$t$, a set $S_{t}$ of sensors is selected, and these sensors transmit
their measurements to a server (base station).



The server then determines a sensing quality $\ensuremath{f}_t(S_t)$
quantifying the utility obtained from the resulting analysis. For
example, if our goal is spatial prediction, the server would build a
model based on the previously collected sensor data, pick a random
sensor $s$, make prediction for the variable ${\mathcal{X}}_{s}$, and then
compare the prediction $\mu_{s}$ with the sensor reading $x_{s}$.  The
error $\ensuremath{f}_{t}=\sigma_{s}^{2}-(\mu_{s}-x_{s})^{2}$ is an unbiased
estimate of the reduction in EMSE.  In the following analysis, we will
only assume that the objective functions $\ensuremath{f}_{t}$ are bounded (w.l.o.g., take values in
$[0,1]$), monotone, and submodular, and that we have some way of
computing $\ensuremath{f}_{t}(S)$ for any subset of sensors $S$.






Our goal is to maximize the total reward obtained by the system 
over $T$ rounds, $\sum_{t=1}^T \ensuremath{f}_t(S_t)$.

























We seek to develop a protocol for selecting the sets $S_{t}$ of
sensors at each round, such that after a small number of rounds the
average performance of our online algorithm converges to the same
performance of the offline strategy (that knows the objective
functions).  We thus compare our protocol against all strategies that
can select a fixed set of $\ensuremath{k}$ sensors for use in all of the rounds;
the best such strategy obtains reward $\max_{S \subseteq V: |S|
\le \ensuremath{k}} \sum_{t=1}^T \ensuremath{f}_t(S)$.  The difference between this quantity
and what our protocol obtains is known as its \emph{regret}, and an
algorithm is said to be \emph{no-regret} if its average regret tends to zero (or less)\footnote{Formally, if $R_T$ is the
  total regret for the first $T$ rounds, no-regret means 
$\limsup_{T \to \infty} R_T/T \le 0$.} as $T \to \infty$.



When $\ensuremath{k}=1$, our problem is
simply the well-studied \emph{multiarmed bandit} (MAB) problem, for
which many no-regret algorithms are known \cite{foster99}.  For
general $\ensuremath{k}$, because the average of several submodular functions
remains submodular, we can apply the result of
Nemhauser~\etal~\cite{nemhauser78} (\emph{cf.}, \secref{sec:offline-problem})
to prove that a simple greedy algorithm obtains a $(1-1/e)$
approximation to the optimal offline solution.




Feige~\cite{feige97} showed that this is optimal in the sense that
obtaining a \\$(1-1/e+\epsilon)$ approximation for any $\epsilon > 0$ is
\class{NP}-hard.  These facts suggest that we cannot expect any efficient
online algorithm to converge to a solution better than\\
$(1-1/e)\max_{S \subseteq V: |S| \le \ensuremath{k}} \sum_{t=1}^T
\ensuremath{f}_t(S)$.  We therefore define the $(1-1/e)$-regret of a sequence of
(possibly random) sets $\set{S_t}_{t=1}^T$ as
\vspace{-0.5em}
\[
\ensuremath{R}_{T} := \paren{1-1/e} \cdot \max_{S \subseteq V: |S| \le \ensuremath{k}}
\sum_{t=1}^T \ensuremath{f}_t(S) \ - \ \sum_{t=1}^T \E{\ensuremath{f}_t(S_t)} 
\]
where the expectation is taken over the distribution for each $S_t$.
We say an online algorithm producing a sequence of sets has 
\emph{no-$(1-1/e)$-regret} if $\limsup_{T \to \infty}
\frac{\ensuremath{R}_{T}}{T} \le 0$.

\item Define sensor selection problem as online optimization problem
\item Objective functions are submodular (examples; mention Nemhauser result)
\item Define $(1-1/e)$-regret
\end{itemize}
}

Distributed Selection of a Single Sensor
\label{sec:sampling}




\ignore{ If we wish to implement a distributed variant of a bandit
algorithm such as {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace, there are two questions we must answer,
namely, how do we sample arms and how do we update the distribution on
arms?  We will now develop a distributed variant of {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace that
solves these challenges.  } 




\commentout{
\andreas{need to move:

  multiarmed bandit problem such that the worst case expected regret
  is
$\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\textsf{OPT} \ensuremath{n} \log \ensuremath{n}} + \textsf{OPT} e^{-\alpha})$, where
  $\textsf{OPT}$ is the total reward of the best action, and in each round at most

Moreover, there is a protocol with worst case expected regret
$\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\textsf{OPT} \ensuremath{n} \log \ensuremath{n}})$ and in each round

$\mathcal{O}(\log \ensuremath{n})$ messages are exchanged with high probability.
\end{theorem}

\ignore{
The key challenge in developing a distributed version of {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace
when sensors can broadcast to all other sensors is to find a way to
sample exactly one element from a probability distribution $p$ over
sensors in a distributed manner.  We measure the cost of the sampling
procedure in terms of the number of broadcast messages.
}

\looseness -1 The key challenge in developing a distributed version of {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace is
to find a way to sample exactly one element from a probability
distribution $p$ over sensors in a distributed manner. This problem is
distinct from randomized leader election \cite{Nakano02}, where the
objective is to select exactly one element but the element need not be
drawn from a specified distribution.  We note that under the multi-hop
communication model, sampling one element from the uniform
distribution given a rooted spanning tree can be done via a simple
random walk~\cite{Kuhn08}, but that under the broadcast and star network models
this approach degenerates to centralized sampling.  
Our algorithm, in contrast, samples from an arbitrary
distribution by allowing sensors to individually decide to activate.
Our bottom-up approach also has two other advantages:
($1$) it is amenable to modification of the activation probabilities based on
local observations, as we discuss in~\secref{sec:measure-dependent-sampling}, and ($2$)
since it does not rely on any global state of the network such as a
spanning tree, it can gracefully cope with significant edge or node
failures.




\ignore{
Our proposed algorithm allows sensors to individually decide to
activate, with the result that the selected sensor is drawn from the
desired distribution.

Our proposed is suited for the broadcast and star network models.

Rooted spanning tree algorithms reduce to centralized sampling in
these models.

Kuhn has proposed a rooted spanning tree algorithm to select an
element of a network uniformly at random.

Kuhn's method assumes a multi-hop network, with rooted spanning tree.

We measure the cost of the sampling procedure in terms of the number
of broadcast messages.
}









\paragraph{A naive distributed sampling scheme}
A naive distributed algorithm would be to let each sensor keep track
of all activation probabilities $p$.  Then, one sensor (e.g., with the
lowest identifier) would broadcast a single random number $u$
uniformly distributed in $[0,1]$, and the sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ for which
$\sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{v}-1} p_{i} \le u < \sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{v}} p_{i}$
would activate.  However, for large sensor network deployments, this
algorithm would require each sensor to store a large amount of global
information (all activation probabilities $p$).  Instead, each sensor
$\ensuremath{v}$ could store only their own probability mass $p_{\ensuremath{v}}$;
the sensors would then, in order of their identifiers, broadcast their
probabilities $p_{\ensuremath{v}}$, and stop once the sum of the
probabilities exceeds $u$.  This approach only requires a constant
amount of local information, but requires an impractical $\Theta(n)$
messages to be sent, and sent sequentially over $\Theta(n)$ time
steps.

\paragraph{Distributed multinomial sampling}
In this section we present a protocol that requires only $\mathcal{O}(1)$
messages in expectation, and only a constant amount of local information.




For a sampling procedure with input distribution $p$, we let $\ensuremath{\hat{p}}$
denote the resulting distribution, where in all cases at most one
sensor is selected, and nothing is selected with probability
$1-\sum_{\ensuremath{v}} \ensuremath{\hat{p}}_{\ensuremath{v}}$.  A simple approach towards
distributed sampling would be to activate each sensor
$\ensuremath{v}\inV$ \emph{independently} from each other with
probability $p_{\ensuremath{v}}$. While in expectation, exactly one sensor is
activated, with probability $\prod_{\ensuremath{v}} (1-p_{\ensuremath{v}})>0$ no
sensor is activated; also since sensors are activated independently,
there is a nonzero probability that more than one sensor is activated.
Using a synchronized clock, the sensors could determine if no sensor
is activated.  In this case, they could simply repeat the selection
procedure until at least one sensor is activated.  
One naive approach would be to repeat the selection
procedure until exactly one sensor is activated.  
However with two sensors and $p_1 = \varepsilon, p_2 = 1 - \varepsilon$ this
algorithm yields $\ensuremath{\hat{p}}_1 = \varepsilon^2 / (1 - 2\varepsilon + 2 \varepsilon^2) =
\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^2)$, so the first sensor is severely underrepresented.
Another simple protocol would be to select exactly one sensor uniformly at
random from the set of activated sensors, which can be implemented using few messages.







\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{|p{7.6cm}|}
\hline
\textbf{The Simple Protocol:}\\
\hspace{0cm} For each sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ in parallel\\
\hspace{0.5cm} Sample $X_{\ensuremath{v}} \sim \Bernoulli{p_{\ensuremath{v}}}$.\\
\hspace{0.5cm} If $(X_{\ensuremath{v}} = 1)$, $X_{\ensuremath{v}}$ activates.\\ 

\hspace{0cm} All active sensors $S$ coordinate to select a single
sensor uniformly at random from $S$, e.g., by electing the minimum ID
sensor in $S$ to do the sampling.\\





\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\noindent
It is not hard to show that with this protocol, for all sensors $\ensuremath{v}$, 
\[
\ensuremath{\hat{p}}_{\ensuremath{v}} = p_{\ensuremath{v}}\cdot \Econd{\frac{1}{|S|}}{\ensuremath{v} \in S} \ge p_{\ensuremath{v}}/ \Econd{|S|}{\ensuremath{v} \in S} \ge
p_{\ensuremath{v}}/2 
\] 
by appealing to Jensen's inequality.  Since $\ensuremath{\hat{p}}_{\ensuremath{v}} \le
p_{\ensuremath{v}}$, we find that this simple protocol maintains a ratio
$r_{\ensuremath{v}} := \ensuremath{\hat{p}}_{\ensuremath{v}} / p_{\ensuremath{v}} \in [\frac12 , 1]$.
Unfortunately, this analysis is tight, as can be seen from the example
with two sensors and $p_1 = \varepsilon, p_2 = 1 - \varepsilon$.


To improve upon the simple protocol, first consider running it on an
example with $p_1 = p_2 = \cdots = p_n = 1/n$.  Since the protocol
behaves exactly the same under permutations of sensor labels, by
symmetry we have $\ensuremath{\hat{p}}_{1} = \ensuremath{\hat{p}}_{2} = \cdots = \ensuremath{\hat{p}}_{n}$, and
thus $r_i = r_j$ for all $i,j$.  Now consider an input distribution
$p$ where there exists integers $N$ and $k_1, k_2, \ldots, k_n$ such
that $p_{\ensuremath{v}} = k_{\ensuremath{v}}/N$ for all $\ensuremath{v}$.  Replace each
$\ensuremath{v}$ with $k_{\ensuremath{v}}$ fictitious sensors, each with probability
mass $1/N$, and each with a label indicating $\ensuremath{v}$.  Run the
simple protocol with the fictitious sensors, selecting a fictitious
sensor $\ensuremath{v}'$, and then actually select the sensor indicated by
the label of $\ensuremath{v}'$.  By symmetry this process selects each
fictitious sensor with probability $(1-\ensuremath{\beta})/N$, where
$\ensuremath{\beta}$ is the probability that nothing at all is selected, and
thus the process selects sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ with probability
$k_{\ensuremath{v}}(1-\ensuremath{\beta})/N = (1-\ensuremath{\beta})p_{\ensuremath{v}}$ (since at most
one fictitious sensor is ever selected).



We may thus consider the following improved protocol which
incorporates the above idea, simulating this modification to the
protocol exactly when $p_{\ensuremath{v}} = k_{\ensuremath{v}}/N$ for all $\ensuremath{v}$.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{|p{7.6cm}|}
\hline
\textbf{The Improved Protocol($N$):}\\
\hspace{0cm} For each sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ in parallel\\
\hspace{0.5cm} Sample $X_{\ensuremath{v}} \sim \Binomial{\ceil{N \cdot
    p_{\ensuremath{v}}}, 1/N}$.\\
\hspace{0.5cm} If $(X_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1)$, then activate sensor $\ensuremath{v}$.\\ 

\hspace{0cm} From the active sensors $S$, select sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ with
probability $X_{\ensuremath{v}}/\sum_{\ensuremath{v}'\in S} X_{\ensuremath{v}'}$.\\






\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

This protocol ensures the ratios $r_{\ensuremath{v}} := \ensuremath{\hat{p}}_{\ensuremath{v}} /
p_{\ensuremath{v}}$ are the same for all sensors, provided each $p_{\ensuremath{v}}$
is a multiple of $1/N$.  Assuming the probabilities are rational,
there will be a sufficiently large $N$ to satisfy this condition.
To reduce $\ensuremath{\beta} := \prob{S = \emptyset}$ in the simple protocol, we
may sample each $X_{\ensuremath{v}}$ from $\Bernoulli{\alpha \cdot p_{\ensuremath{v}}}$ for any
$\alpha \in [1, n]$.  The symmetry argument remains unchanged.
This in turn suggests sampling $X_{\ensuremath{v}}$ from 
$\Binomial{\ceil{N \cdot p_{\ensuremath{v}}}, \alpha/N}$ in the improved
protocol.  Taking the limit as $N \to \infty$, the binomial
distribution becomes Poisson, and we obtain the desired protocol.


\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{|p{8.2cm}|}
\hline
\textbf{The Poisson Multinomial Sampling (PMS)
  Protocol($\alpha$):}\\
\hspace{0cm} Same as the improved protocol, except each \\ 
\hspace{0cm} sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ samples $X_{\ensuremath{v}} \sim \Poisson{\alpha p_{\ensuremath{v}} }$\\
\ignore{
\hspace{0cm} \emph{Sensors:} \\
\hspace{0cm} For each sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ in parallel\\
\hspace{0.5cm} Sample $X_{\ensuremath{v}} \sim \Poisson{\alpha p_{\ensuremath{v}} }$.\\
\hspace{0.5cm} If $(X_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1)$, send $X_{\ensuremath{v}}$ to the server.\\ 

\hspace{0cm} \emph{Server:}\\
\hspace{0cm} Receive messages from a set $S$ of sensors. \\
\hspace{0cm} If $S = \emptyset$, select nothing.\\
\hspace{0cm} Else, select $\ensuremath{v}$ with probability
$X_{\ensuremath{v}}/\sum_{\ensuremath{v}' \in S} X_{\ensuremath{v}'}$.\\
}
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}
\noindent
Straight-forward calculation shows that 
\[
\prob{S = \emptyset}  = \prod_{\ensuremath{v}} \exp\set{ - \alpha \cdot
  p_{\ensuremath{v}}}  = \exp \bigl\{ - \sum_{\ensuremath{v}} \alpha \cdot p_{\ensuremath{v}}\bigr\}  = e^{-\alpha}  
\]
\ignore{
\begin{align*}
\prob{S = \emptyset}  

&= \prod_{\ensuremath{v}} \exp\set{ - \alpha \cdot p_{\ensuremath{v}}} \\
& = \exp \bigl\{ - \sum_{\ensuremath{v}} \alpha \cdot p_{\ensuremath{v}}\bigr\}  = \exp \set{-\alpha}   
\end{align*}
} 
Let $C$ be the number of messages.  Then 
\[ \E{C} =  \sum_{\ensuremath{v}} \prob{X_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1} =  \sum_{\ensuremath{v}}
(1-e^{-\alpha p_{\ensuremath{v}}}) \le \sum_{\ensuremath{v}} \alpha p_{\ensuremath{v}}   =
\alpha \]
\ignore{
\begin{align*}
\E{C} & =  \sum_{\ensuremath{v}} \prob{X_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1} \\
 & = \sum_{\ensuremath{v}} (1-\exp\set{-\alpha p_{\ensuremath{v}}})\\
 & \le  \sum_{\ensuremath{v}} \alpha p_{\ensuremath{v}} = \alpha\mbox{.}
\end{align*}
Here we have used linearity of expectation in the first line, and $1+x
\le e^x$ for all $x \in \mathbb R$ in the third.
} 
Here we have used linearity of expectation, and $1+x
\le e^x$ for all $x \in \mathbb R$.
In summary, we have the following result about our protocol:
\begin{prop} \label{thm:sampling}
Fix any fixed  $p$ and $\alpha>0$.  The \LimitProtocolShort always selects at most
one sensor, ensures   



$$\forall \ensuremath{v}:\ \prob{\ensuremath{v} \text{ selected}} = (1 - e^{-\alpha})p_{\ensuremath{v}}$$
and requires no more than $\alpha$ messages in expectation. 
\end{prop}






In order to ensure that exactly one sensor is selected, whenever $S =
\emptyset$ we can simply rerun the protocol with fresh random seeds as
many times as needed until $S$ is non-empty.  Using $\alpha = 1$, 
this modification will require only $\mathcal{O}(1)$ messages in expectation and
at most $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$ messages with high probability in the broadcast model.
We can combine this protocol with {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace to get the following
result.




\begin{theorem} \label{thm:distributed-single-sensor-selection}








In the broadcast model, running {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace using the \LimitProtocolShort with
$\alpha = 1$, and rerunning the protocol whenever nothing is selected,
yields exactly the same regret bound as standard {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace, and
 in each round at most $e/(e-1)+2 \approx 3.582$ messages
are broadcast in expectation.



\end{theorem}

The regret bound for {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace is $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\textsf{OPT} \ensuremath{n} \log \ensuremath{n}})$, where
$\textsf{OPT}$ is the total reward of the best action.  
Our variant simulates {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace, and thus has identical regret.


Proofs of our theoretical results can be found in\ifthenelse{\boolean{istechrpt}}{
\noindent
the
Appendix. }{ 
the full version of this paper
\cite{golovin09distributed}.  }


\paragraph{Remark} Running our variant of {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace requires that
each sensor know the number of sensors, $n$, in order to compute its
activation probability.  If each sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ has only a reasonable
estimate of $n_{\ensuremath{v}}$ of $n$, however, our algorithm still
performs well.  
For example, it is possible to prove that if all of the sensors have
the same estimate $n_{\ensuremath{v}} = cn$ for some constant $c > 0$, 
then the upper bound on expected 
regret, $R(c)$, grows as $R(c) \approx  R(1)\cdot \max \set{c,
  1/c}$.



The expected number of activations in this
case increases by at most $\paren{\frac{1}{c} - 1}\gamma$.
In general underestimating $n$ leads to more activations, and
underestimating or overestimating $n$ can lead to more regret.
This graceful degradation of performance with respect to the error
in estimating $n$ holds for all of our algorithms.

items.clean: Observation dependent activation We also experimentally evaluate our algofontOD-DOGxspace algorithm with observation specific sensor activations. We choose different values for the activation cost c_v, which we vary as multiples of the total achievable reward. The activation cost c_v lets us smoothly trade off the average number of sensors activating each round and the average obtained reward. The resulting activation strategies are used to select a subset of size k=10 from a collection of 12,527 sensors. figreffig:waterfixed presents rates of convergence using the algofontOD-DOGxspace algorithm under a fixed objective function which considers all contamination events. In figreffig:watervarying, convergence rates are presented under a varying objective function, which selects a different contamination event on each round. For low activation costs, the performance quickly converges to or exceeds the performance of the offline solution. Even under the lowest activation costs in our experiments, the average number of extra activations per stage in the algofontOD-DOGxspace algorithm is at most 5. These results indicate that observation specific activation can lead to drastically improved performance at small additional activation cost. subfigure[[T] Convergence] includegraphics[width=0.48textwidth,height=0.24textwidth]fig/F-temp-conv-g0-01-d10-k5-500000 subfigure[[R] Convergence] includegraphics[width=0.48textwidth,height=0.24textwidth]fig/F-rain-conv-g0-01-d10-k5-500000 subfigure[[W] Constant Objective] includegraphics[width=0.48textwidth,height=0.24textwidth]fig/formatted_OD-vs-activation-cost_Fwater__20-23-58 subfigure[[W] Varying Objective] includegraphics[width=0.48textwidth,height=0.24textwidth]fig/formattedOD-vs-activation-cost_FwaterTimeVarying__00-13-30 captionfootnotesize Experimental results on [T] Temperature data, [R] precipitation data and [W] water distribution network data.

Furthermore, this conditional distribution quantifies the
\emph{uncertainty} in the prediction: Intuitively, we would like to
select sensors that minimize the predictive uncertainty.  One way to
quantify the predictive uncertainty is the mean squared prediction
error,
$$\MSE({\mathcal{X}}_{V\setminus{\mathcal{A}}}\mid {\mathbf{x}}_{{\mathcal{A}}}) =
\frac{1}{\ensuremath{n}}\sum_{s\inV\setminus{\mathcal{A}}}
\mathbb{E}[({\mathcal{X}}_s-\mathbb{E}[{\mathcal{X}}_{s}\mid{\mathbf{x}}_{{\mathcal{A}}}])^{2}\mid
{\mathbf{x}}_{{\mathcal{A}}}].$$ In general, the measurements ${\mathbf{x}}_{{\mathcal{A}}}$ that sensors
${\mathcal{A}}$ will make is not known in advance.  Thus, we can base our
optimization on the \emph{expected mean squared prediction error},
$$\EMSE({\mathcal{A}}) = \int dp({\mathbf{x}}_{{\mathcal{A}}}) \MSE({\mathcal{X}}_{V\setminus{\mathcal{A}}}\mid {\mathbf{x}}_{{\mathcal{A}}}).$$
Equivalently, we can maximize the \emph{reduction} in mean squared prediction error,
$$f_{\EMSE}({\mathcal{A}}) = \EMSE(\emptyset)-\EMSE({\mathcal{A}}).$$ By definition,
$f_{\EMSE}(\emptyset)=0$, i.e., no sensors obtain no
utility. Furthermore, $f_{\EMSE}$ is monotonic: if
${\mathcal{A}}\subseteq{\mathcal{B}}\subseteqV$, then $f_{\EMSE}({\mathcal{A}})\leq
f_{\EMSE}({\mathcal{B}})$, i.e., adding more sensors always helps.  That means,
$f_{\EMSE}$ is maximized by the set of all sensors $V$.  However,
in practice, we would like to only select a small set of, e.g., at
most $k$ sensors due to bandwidth and power constraints:
$${\mathcal{A}}^*=\argmax_{{\mathcal{A}}}f_{\EMSE}({\mathcal{A}})\text{ s.t. }|{\mathcal{A}}|\leq k.$$
Unfortunately, this optimization problem is NP-hard, so we cannot
expect to efficiently find the optimal solution.  Fortunately, it can
be shown \cite{das07} that in many settings\footnote{For Gaussian
models and conditional suppressorfreeness \cite{das07}}, the function
$f_{\EMSE}$ satisfies an intuitive diminishing returns property called
submodularity.  A set function $f:2^{V}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$
is called \emph{submodular}

full.raw:
The Online Sensor Selection Problem
\label{sec:online-problem}






We now consider the more challenging problem where the objective
function is not specified in advance, and needs to be learned during
the monitoring task.  We assume that we intend to monitor the
environment for a number $T$ of time steps (rounds).  In each round
$t$, a set $S_{t}$ of sensors is selected, and these sensors transmit
their measurements to a server (base station).



The server then determines a sensing quality $\ensuremath{f}_t(S_t)$
quantifying the utility obtained from the resulting analysis. For
example, if our goal is spatial prediction, the server would build a
model based on the previously collected sensor data, pick a random
sensor $s$, make prediction for the variable ${\mathcal{X}}_{s}$, and then
compare the prediction $\mu_{s}$ with the sensor reading $x_{s}$.  The
error $\ensuremath{f}_{t}=\sigma_{s}^{2}-(\mu_{s}-x_{s})^{2}$ is an unbiased
estimate of the reduction in EMSE.  In the following analysis, we will
only assume that the objective functions $\ensuremath{f}_{t}$ are bounded (w.l.o.g., take values in
$[0,1]$), monotone, and submodular, and that we have some way of
computing $\ensuremath{f}_{t}(S)$ for any subset of sensors $S$.






Our goal is to maximize the total reward obtained by the system 
over $T$ rounds, $\sum_{t=1}^T \ensuremath{f}_t(S_t)$.

























We seek to develop a protocol for selecting the sets $S_{t}$ of
sensors at each round, such that after a small number of rounds the
average performance of our online algorithm converges to the same
performance of the offline strategy (that knows the objective
functions).  We thus compare our protocol against all strategies that
can select a fixed set of $\ensuremath{k}$ sensors for use in all of the rounds;
the best such strategy obtains reward $\max_{S \subseteq V: |S|
\le \ensuremath{k}} \sum_{t=1}^T \ensuremath{f}_t(S)$.  The difference between this quantity
and what our protocol obtains is known as its \emph{regret}, and an
algorithm is said to be \emph{no-regret} if its average regret tends to zero (or less)\footnote{Formally, if $R_T$ is the
  total regret for the first $T$ rounds, no-regret means 
$\limsup_{T \to \infty} R_T/T \le 0$.} as $T \to \infty$.



When $\ensuremath{k}=1$, our problem is
simply the well-studied \emph{multiarmed bandit} (MAB) problem, for
which many no-regret algorithms are known \cite{foster99}.  For
general $\ensuremath{k}$, because the average of several submodular functions
remains submodular, we can apply the result of
Nemhauser~\etal~\cite{nemhauser78} (\emph{cf.}, \secref{sec:offline-problem})
to prove that a simple greedy algorithm obtains a $(1-1/e)$
approximation to the optimal offline solution.




Feige~\cite{feige97} showed that this is optimal in the sense that
obtaining a \\$(1-1/e+\epsilon)$ approximation for any $\epsilon > 0$ is
\class{NP}-hard.  These facts suggest that we cannot expect any efficient
online algorithm to converge to a solution better than\\
$(1-1/e)\max_{S \subseteq V: |S| \le \ensuremath{k}} \sum_{t=1}^T
\ensuremath{f}_t(S)$.  We therefore define the $(1-1/e)$-regret of a sequence of
(possibly random) sets $\set{S_t}_{t=1}^T$ as
\vspace{-0.5em}
\[
\ensuremath{R}_{T} := \paren{1-1/e} \cdot \max_{S \subseteq V: |S| \le \ensuremath{k}}
\sum_{t=1}^T \ensuremath{f}_t(S) \ - \ \sum_{t=1}^T \E{\ensuremath{f}_t(S_t)} 
\]
where the expectation is taken over the distribution for each $S_t$.
We say an online algorithm producing a sequence of sets has 
\emph{no-$(1-1/e)$-regret} if $\limsup_{T \to \infty}
\frac{\ensuremath{R}_{T}}{T} \le 0$.

\begin{proof}
Lazy renormalization
selects each sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ with probability
$(1-e^{-\alpha})p_{\ensuremath{v}}$, because of the way the random bits
$r_{\ensuremath{v}}$ are shared in order to implement a coupled distribution for
sensor activation and selection.
Note that it would be sufficient to run the \LimitProtocol on the correct (possibly
oversampled) probabilities, $\alpha p_{\ensuremath{v}}$, 
since then~\propref{thm:sampling} ensures that each $\ensuremath{v}$
is selected with probability $(1 - e^{-\alpha}) p_{\ensuremath{v}}$.
The difficulty is that $\ensuremath{v}$ does not have access to the correct
normalizer $Z(t)$, but only its estimate (lower bound) for it,
$Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$.
To overcome this difficulty, we define a joint probability
distribution over two random variables $(X_{\ensuremath{v}},
Y_{\ensuremath{v}})$, where 
\[
X_{\ensuremath{v}}  = X_{\ensuremath{v}}(R) := \left\{ 
\begin{array}{ll} 
1 & \text{if $R \ge 1 - \alpha \cdot\rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t))$} \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{array}  \right.
\]
\[
Y_{\ensuremath{v}} = Y_{\ensuremath{v}}(R) := \min \set{b \ :\ \sum_{a=0}^b \frac{e^{-\lambda}
    \lambda^{a}}{a!} \ge R }
\]
and $\lambda := \alpha \cdot \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z(t))$, and $R$ is
sampled uniformly at random from $[0,1]$.
Now, note that $Y_{\ensuremath{v}}$ is distributed as $\Poisson{\lambda}$.
Also note that $Y_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1$ implies $X_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1$,
because $Y_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1$ implies $R \ge e^{-\lambda}$ and 
\[
 e^{-\lambda}  \ge 1 - \lambda \ge 1 - \alpha \cdot \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t))
\]
since $1 + x \le e^x$ for all $x \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$, and $\rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t),
Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)) \ge \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z(t))$ due to fact
that $Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) \le Z(t)$.
It follows that we can use the event $X_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1$ as a
conservative indicator that $\ensuremath{v}$ should activate.
In this case, it will send its sampled value for $R$, namely
$r_{\ensuremath{v}}$, and its weight $w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$ to the server.  
The server knows $Z(t)$, and then can
use $r_{\ensuremath{v}}$ and $w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$ to compute
$Y_{\ensuremath{v}}(r_{\ensuremath{v}})$, 
the sample from $\Poisson{\lambda}$ that $\ensuremath{v}$ would have
drawn had it known $Z(t)$.  The resulting distribution on selected
sensors is thus exactly the same as in the \LimitProtocol without lazy
renormalization.
Invoking~\propref{thm:sampling} thus completes the proof.

\begin{theorem} \label{thm:faulty-sensors}
Fix finite set $V$, $\ensuremath{k} \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$, and a sequence of 
monotone submodular functions $f_1, \ldots, f_T:2^{V} \to [0,1]$.
Let $\textsf{OPT}_{\ensuremath{k}} = \max_{S \subset V, |S| \le \ensuremath{k}} \sum_{t=1}^{t} f_t(S)$.
For all $\ensuremath{v} \in V$ let $\ensuremath{v}'$ be a random element which is 
$v$ with probability $1-\delta_\ensuremath{v}$ and is $\textsf{null}$\footnote{Here,
  a $\textsf{null}$ element always contributes nothing in the way of utility,
  so that $f_t(S \cup \set{\textsf{null}}) = f_t(S)$ for all $t$ and $S$.}
 with probability
$\delta_\ensuremath{v}$.  
Let $f'_t(S') := \E{f_t(S)}$ where $S$ the set obtained
by including every element $\ensuremath{v}'$ of $S'$ in it independently with
probability $\delta_{\ensuremath{v}}$.
Let $S'_1, \ldots, S'_T$ be the sequence of random sets obtained from
running $\algofont{OG}_{\algofont{unit}}$\xspace with actions $V' := \set{\ensuremath{v}' : \ensuremath{v} \in
  V}$ and objective functions $\set{f'_t}_{t = 1}^T$ and $\ensuremath{k}' =
\ensuremath{k}/(1-\delta)$ stages, where $\delta = \max_{\ensuremath{v}}
\delta_{\ensuremath{v}}$.
Suppose the algorithms for each stage have expected regret at most $r$.
Then 
\[
\E{\sum_{t=1}^T f'_t(S'_t)} \ge \paren{1-\frac{1}{e}}\textsf{OPT}_{\ensuremath{k}} - \ceil{\frac{\ensuremath{k}}{1-\delta}} r\mbox{.}
\]
\end{theorem}

The key challenge in developing a distributed version of {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace
when sensors can broadcast to all other sensors is to find a way to
sample exactly one element from a probability distribution $p$ over
sensors in a distributed manner.  We measure the cost of the sampling
procedure in terms of the number of broadcast messages.
}

\looseness -1 The key challenge in developing a distributed version of {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace is
to find a way to sample exactly one element from a probability
distribution $p$ over sensors in a distributed manner. This problem is
distinct from randomized leader election \cite{Nakano02}, where the
objective is to select exactly one element but the element need not be
drawn from a specified distribution.  We note that under the multi-hop
communication model, sampling one element from the uniform
distribution given a rooted spanning tree can be done via a simple
random walk~\cite{Kuhn08}, but that under the broadcast and star network models
this approach degenerates to centralized sampling.  
Our algorithm, in contrast, samples from an arbitrary
distribution by allowing sensors to individually decide to activate.
Our bottom-up approach also has two other advantages:
($1$) it is amenable to modification of the activation probabilities based on
local observations, as we discuss in~\secref{sec:measure-dependent-sampling}, and ($2$)
since it does not rely on any global state of the network such as a
spanning tree, it can gracefully cope with significant edge or node
failures.




\ignore{
Our proposed algorithm allows sensors to individually decide to
activate, with the result that the selected sensor is drawn from the
desired distribution.

Our proposed is suited for the broadcast and star network models.

Rooted spanning tree algorithms reduce to centralized sampling in
these models.

Kuhn has proposed a rooted spanning tree algorithm to select an
element of a network uniformly at random.

Kuhn's method assumes a multi-hop network, with rooted spanning tree.

We measure the cost of the sampling procedure in terms of the number
of broadcast messages.
}









\paragraph{A naive distributed sampling scheme}
A naive distributed algorithm would be to let each sensor keep track
of all activation probabilities $p$.  Then, one sensor (e.g., with the
lowest identifier) would broadcast a single random number $u$
uniformly distributed in $[0,1]$, and the sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ for which
$\sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{v}-1} p_{i} \le u < \sum_{i=1}^{\ensuremath{v}} p_{i}$
would activate.  However, for large sensor network deployments, this
algorithm would require each sensor to store a large amount of global
information (all activation probabilities $p$).  Instead, each sensor
$\ensuremath{v}$ could store only their own probability mass $p_{\ensuremath{v}}$;
the sensors would then, in order of their identifiers, broadcast their
probabilities $p_{\ensuremath{v}}$, and stop once the sum of the
probabilities exceeds $u$.  This approach only requires a constant
amount of local information, but requires an impractical $\Theta(n)$
messages to be sent, and sent sequentially over $\Theta(n)$ time
steps.

\paragraph{Distributed multinomial sampling}
In this section we present a protocol that requires only $\mathcal{O}(1)$
messages in expectation, and only a constant amount of local information.




For a sampling procedure with input distribution $p$, we let $\ensuremath{\hat{p}}$
denote the resulting distribution, where in all cases at most one
sensor is selected, and nothing is selected with probability
$1-\sum_{\ensuremath{v}} \ensuremath{\hat{p}}_{\ensuremath{v}}$.  A simple approach towards
distributed sampling would be to activate each sensor
$\ensuremath{v}\inV$ \emph{independently} from each other with
probability $p_{\ensuremath{v}}$. While in expectation, exactly one sensor is
activated, with probability $\prod_{\ensuremath{v}} (1-p_{\ensuremath{v}})>0$ no
sensor is activated; also since sensors are activated independently,
there is a nonzero probability that more than one sensor is activated.
Using a synchronized clock, the sensors could determine if no sensor
is activated.  In this case, they could simply repeat the selection
procedure until at least one sensor is activated.  
One naive approach would be to repeat the selection
procedure until exactly one sensor is activated.  
However with two sensors and $p_1 = \varepsilon, p_2 = 1 - \varepsilon$ this
algorithm yields $\ensuremath{\hat{p}}_1 = \varepsilon^2 / (1 - 2\varepsilon + 2 \varepsilon^2) =
\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^2)$, so the first sensor is severely underrepresented.
Another simple protocol would be to select exactly one sensor uniformly at
random from the set of activated sensors, which can be implemented using few messages.







\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{|p{7.6cm}|}
\hline
\textbf{The Simple Protocol:}\\
\hspace{0cm} For each sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ in parallel\\
\hspace{0.5cm} Sample $X_{\ensuremath{v}} \sim \Bernoulli{p_{\ensuremath{v}}}$.\\
\hspace{0.5cm} If $(X_{\ensuremath{v}} = 1)$, $X_{\ensuremath{v}}$ activates.\\ 

\hspace{0cm} All active sensors $S$ coordinate to select a single
sensor uniformly at random from $S$, e.g., by electing the minimum ID
sensor in $S$ to do the sampling.\\





\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\noindent
It is not hard to show that with this protocol, for all sensors $\ensuremath{v}$, 
\[
\ensuremath{\hat{p}}_{\ensuremath{v}} = p_{\ensuremath{v}}\cdot \Econd{\frac{1}{|S|}}{\ensuremath{v} \in S} \ge p_{\ensuremath{v}}/ \Econd{|S|}{\ensuremath{v} \in S} \ge
p_{\ensuremath{v}}/2 
\] 
by appealing to Jensen's inequality.  Since $\ensuremath{\hat{p}}_{\ensuremath{v}} \le
p_{\ensuremath{v}}$, we find that this simple protocol maintains a ratio
$r_{\ensuremath{v}} := \ensuremath{\hat{p}}_{\ensuremath{v}} / p_{\ensuremath{v}} \in [\frac12 , 1]$.
Unfortunately, this analysis is tight, as can be seen from the example
with two sensors and $p_1 = \varepsilon, p_2 = 1 - \varepsilon$.


To improve upon the simple protocol, first consider running it on an
example with $p_1 = p_2 = \cdots = p_n = 1/n$.  Since the protocol
behaves exactly the same under permutations of sensor labels, by
symmetry we have $\ensuremath{\hat{p}}_{1} = \ensuremath{\hat{p}}_{2} = \cdots = \ensuremath{\hat{p}}_{n}$, and
thus $r_i = r_j$ for all $i,j$.  Now consider an input distribution
$p$ where there exists integers $N$ and $k_1, k_2, \ldots, k_n$ such
that $p_{\ensuremath{v}} = k_{\ensuremath{v}}/N$ for all $\ensuremath{v}$.  Replace each
$\ensuremath{v}$ with $k_{\ensuremath{v}}$ fictitious sensors, each with probability
mass $1/N$, and each with a label indicating $\ensuremath{v}$.  Run the
simple protocol with the fictitious sensors, selecting a fictitious
sensor $\ensuremath{v}'$, and then actually select the sensor indicated by
the label of $\ensuremath{v}'$.  By symmetry this process selects each
fictitious sensor with probability $(1-\ensuremath{\beta})/N$, where
$\ensuremath{\beta}$ is the probability that nothing at all is selected, and
thus the process selects sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ with probability
$k_{\ensuremath{v}}(1-\ensuremath{\beta})/N = (1-\ensuremath{\beta})p_{\ensuremath{v}}$ (since at most
one fictitious sensor is ever selected).



We may thus consider the following improved protocol which
incorporates the above idea, simulating this modification to the
protocol exactly when $p_{\ensuremath{v}} = k_{\ensuremath{v}}/N$ for all $\ensuremath{v}$.

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{|p{7.6cm}|}
\hline
\textbf{The Improved Protocol($N$):}\\
\hspace{0cm} For each sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ in parallel\\
\hspace{0.5cm} Sample $X_{\ensuremath{v}} \sim \Binomial{\ceil{N \cdot
    p_{\ensuremath{v}}}, 1/N}$.\\
\hspace{0.5cm} If $(X_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1)$, then activate sensor $\ensuremath{v}$.\\ 

\hspace{0cm} From the active sensors $S$, select sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ with
probability $X_{\ensuremath{v}}/\sum_{\ensuremath{v}'\in S} X_{\ensuremath{v}'}$.\\






\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

This protocol ensures the ratios $r_{\ensuremath{v}} := \ensuremath{\hat{p}}_{\ensuremath{v}} /
p_{\ensuremath{v}}$ are the same for all sensors, provided each $p_{\ensuremath{v}}$
is a multiple of $1/N$.  Assuming the probabilities are rational,
there will be a sufficiently large $N$ to satisfy this condition.
To reduce $\ensuremath{\beta} := \prob{S = \emptyset}$ in the simple protocol, we
may sample each $X_{\ensuremath{v}}$ from $\Bernoulli{\alpha \cdot p_{\ensuremath{v}}}$ for any
$\alpha \in [1, n]$.  The symmetry argument remains unchanged.
This in turn suggests sampling $X_{\ensuremath{v}}$ from 
$\Binomial{\ceil{N \cdot p_{\ensuremath{v}}}, \alpha/N}$ in the improved
protocol.  Taking the limit as $N \to \infty$, the binomial
distribution becomes Poisson, and we obtain the desired protocol.

\paragraph{Remark} Running our variant of {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace requires that
each sensor know the number of sensors, $n$, in order to compute its
activation probability.  If each sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ has only a reasonable
estimate of $n_{\ensuremath{v}}$ of $n$, however, our algorithm still
performs well.  
For example, it is possible to prove that if all of the sensors have
the same estimate $n_{\ensuremath{v}} = cn$ for some constant $c > 0$, 
then the upper bound on expected 
regret, $R(c)$, grows as $R(c) \approx  R(1)\cdot \max \set{c,
  1/c}$.



The expected number of activations in this
case increases by at most $\paren{\frac{1}{c} - 1}\gamma$.
In general underestimating $n$ leads to more activations, and
underestimating or overestimating $n$ can lead to more regret.
This graceful degradation of performance with respect to the error
in estimating $n$ holds for all of our algorithms.

Let $X_{\ensuremath{v}} \sim \Bernoulli{\alpha \cdot p_{\ensuremath{v}}}$ be the indicator random
variable for the activation of $\ensuremath{v}$, and let $X := \sum_{\ensuremath{v}}
X_{\ensuremath{v}}$.  The expected number of sensor activations is then
\[
\E{X \ |\ X \ge 1} = \E{X}/\prob{X \ge 1} \mbox{.}
\]
In the limit as $\max_{\ensuremath{v}} p_{\ensuremath{v}}$ tends to zero, $X$
converges to a Poisson random variable with mean $\alpha$.
In this case, $\frac{\E{X}}{\prob{X \ge 1}} = \alpha / (1 - e^{-\alpha})$
To see that this is an upper bound, consider an arbitrary distribution
$p$ on the sensors, and fix some $\ensuremath{v}$ with $x := p_{\ensuremath{v}} > 0$.
We claim that replacing $\ensuremath{v}$ with two sensors $\ensuremath{v}_1$ and
$\ensuremath{v}_2$ with positive probability mass $x_1$ and
$x_2$ with $x = x_1+x_2$ can only serve to increase the expected number of
sensor activations, because $\E{X}$ is unchanged, and $\prob{X \ge 1}$
decreases.  The latter is true essentially because 
$\prob{\exists i \in \set{1,2}: \ensuremath{v}_i \text{ activates}} = 1 -
(1-x_1)(1-x_2) = x - x_1x_2 < x$.  To complete the proof, notice that 
repeating this process with $\ensuremath{v} = \argmax (p_{\ensuremath{v}})$ and $x_i = x/2$ ensures $X$
converges to a Poisson variable with mean $\alpha$, while only
increasing $\E{X \ |\ X \ge 1}$.

\begin{proof}
Lazy renormalization
selects each sensor $\ensuremath{v}$ with probability
$(1-e^{-\alpha})p_{\ensuremath{v}}$, because of the way the random bits
$r_{\ensuremath{v}}$ are shared in order to implement a coupled distribution for
sensor activation and selection.
Note that it would be sufficient to run the \LimitProtocol on the correct (possibly
oversampled) probabilities, $\alpha p_{\ensuremath{v}}$, 
since then~\propref{thm:sampling} ensures that each $\ensuremath{v}$
is selected with probability $(1 - e^{-\alpha}) p_{\ensuremath{v}}$.
The difficulty is that $\ensuremath{v}$ does not have access to the correct
normalizer $Z(t)$, but only its estimate (lower bound) for it,
$Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$.
To overcome this difficulty, we define a joint probability
distribution over two random variables $(X_{\ensuremath{v}},
Y_{\ensuremath{v}})$, where 
\[
X_{\ensuremath{v}}  = X_{\ensuremath{v}}(R) := \left\{ 
\begin{array}{ll} 
1 & \text{if $R \ge 1 - \alpha \cdot\rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t))$} \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{array}  \right.
\]
\[
Y_{\ensuremath{v}} = Y_{\ensuremath{v}}(R) := \min \set{b \ :\ \sum_{a=0}^b \frac{e^{-\lambda}
    \lambda^{a}}{a!} \ge R }
\]
and $\lambda := \alpha \cdot \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z(t))$, and $R$ is
sampled uniformly at random from $[0,1]$.
Now, note that $Y_{\ensuremath{v}}$ is distributed as $\Poisson{\lambda}$.
Also note that $Y_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1$ implies $X_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1$,
because $Y_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1$ implies $R \ge e^{-\lambda}$ and 
\[
 e^{-\lambda}  \ge 1 - \lambda \ge 1 - \alpha \cdot \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t))
\]
since $1 + x \le e^x$ for all $x \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}$, and $\rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t),
Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)) \ge \rho(w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t), Z(t))$ due to fact
that $Z_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) \le Z(t)$.
It follows that we can use the event $X_{\ensuremath{v}} \ge 1$ as a
conservative indicator that $\ensuremath{v}$ should activate.
In this case, it will send its sampled value for $R$, namely
$r_{\ensuremath{v}}$, and its weight $w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$ to the server.  
The server knows $Z(t)$, and then can
use $r_{\ensuremath{v}}$ and $w_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$ to compute
$Y_{\ensuremath{v}}(r_{\ensuremath{v}})$, 
the sample from $\Poisson{\lambda}$ that $\ensuremath{v}$ would have
drawn had it known $Z(t)$.  The resulting distribution on selected
sensors is thus exactly the same as in the \LimitProtocol without lazy
renormalization.
Invoking~\propref{thm:sampling} thus completes the proof.
\end{proof}


We now describe the assumptions that are sufficient to ensure lazy
renormalization has low communication costs.
Fix an action $\ensuremath{v}$ and a multiarmed bandit algorithm.
Let $p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) \in [0,1]$ be the random variable denoting the
probability the algorithm assigns to $\ensuremath{v}$ on round $t$.
The value of $p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$ depends on the random choices made by
the algorithm and the payoffs observed by it on previous rounds.
We assume the following about each $p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$ can be computed from local information
  $\ensuremath{v}$ possesses and global information the server has.
\item There exists an $\epsilon > 0$ such that $p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)
  \ge \epsilon$ for all $t$.
\item $p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) < p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t+1)$ implies $\ensuremath{v}$ was
  selected in round $t$.
\item There exists $\hat{\epsilon} > 0$ such that 
  $p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t+1) \ge p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)/(1+\hat{\epsilon})$ for all $t$.
\end{enumerate}
Many MAB algorithms satisfy these conditions.
For example, all MAB algorithms with non-trivial no-regret guarantees
against adversarial payoff functions must continually explore all
their options, which effectively mandates $p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t) \ge
\epsilon$ for some $\epsilon > 0$.  In Lemma~\ref{lem:exp3conditions}
we prove that {\algofont{EXP3}}\xspace does so with $\epsilon = \gamma/\ensuremath{n}$ and
$\hat{\epsilon} = (e-1)\frac{\gamma}{\ensuremath{n}}$, assuming payoffs in $[0,1]$.
In this case, Theorem~\ref{thm:lazy_renorm_ratio} bounds the expected
increase in sensor communications due to lazy renormalization by a
factor of $1  + \frac{e-1}{\alpha}$.

\begin{proof}
Fix $\ensuremath{v}$, and let $p(t) := p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$, $q(t) := q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)$.
We begin by bounding $\prob{q(t) \ge \lambda p(t)}$ for $\lambda \ge
1$.  Let $t_0$ be the most recent round in which $q(t_0) = p(t_0)$.
We assume $q(0) = p(0)$, so $t_0$ exists.
Then $q(t) = p(t_0) \ge \lambda p(t)$  implies $p(t_0)/p(t)
\ge \lambda$.  By assumption $p(t')/p(t'+1) \le (1+\hat{\epsilon})$
for all $t'$, so $p(t_0)/p(t) \le (1+\hat{\epsilon})^{t-t_0}$.
Thus $\lambda \le (1+\hat{\epsilon})^{t-t_0}$ and 
$t-t_0 \ge \ln(\lambda)/ \ln (1+\hat{\epsilon})$. 
Define $t(\lambda) := \ln(\lambda)/ \ln (1+\hat{\epsilon})$.


By definition of $t_0$, there were no activations under lazy renormalization in rounds $t_0$
through $t-1$ inclusive, which occurs with probability 
$\prod_{t' = t_0}^{t-1} (1-\alpha q(t'))$ $=$ $(1-\alpha
q(t))^{t-t_{0}} $ $\le$ $(1-\alpha q(t))^{\ceil{t(\lambda)}}$, where $\alpha$ is the
oversampling parameter in the protocol.  


We now bound $\Econd{q(t)/p(t)}{q(t)}$.
Recall that $\E{X} = \int_{x = 0}^{\infty} \prob{X \ge x}dx$ for any non-negative
random variable $X$.  It will also be convenient to define 
$\ensuremath{\omega} := \ln(1/(1 - \alpha q(t))) / \ln(1+\hat{\epsilon})$ and assume for now
that $\ensuremath{\omega} > 1$.
Conditioning on $q(t)$, we see that 
\[
\begin{array}{lcl}
 \vspace{2mm}
\Econd{q(t)/p(t)}{q(t)} & = & \int_{\lambda = 0}^{\infty} \prob{q(t) \ge
  \lambda p(t)}d\lambda \\ 
 \vspace{2mm}
  & = & 1 + \int_{\lambda = 1}^{\infty} \prob{q(t) \ge
  \lambda p(t)}d\lambda \\ 
\vspace{2mm}
 & \le & 1 + \int_{\lambda = 1}^{\infty} (1-\alpha q(t))^{t(\lambda)}d\lambda\\
 \vspace{2mm}
 & = & 1 + \int_{\lambda = 1}^{\infty}
\lambda^{\ln(1-\alpha q(t))/\ln(1+\hat{\epsilon}) }d\lambda \\
 \vspace{2mm}

 & = & 1 + \frac{1}{\ensuremath{\omega} - 1}


\end{array}
\]

$\ln(1+x) \le x$ for all $x > -1$, we can show that 


$\ensuremath{\omega} \ge \alpha q(t)/\hat{\epsilon}$
so $1+\frac{1}{\ensuremath{\omega} - 1} \le \alpha
q(t)/(\alpha q(t) - \hat{\epsilon})$.
Thus, if $\alpha q(t) > \hat{\epsilon}$ then $\ensuremath{\omega} > 1$ and we
obtain 
$\Econd{q(t)/p(t)}{q(t)} \le  \alpha q(t)/(\alpha q(t) - \hat{\epsilon})$.


If $q(t) >> \hat{\epsilon}$, this gives a good bound.  If $q(t)$ is small, we
rely on the assumption that $p(t) \ge \epsilon$ for all $t$ to get a trivial
bound of $q(t)/p(t) \le q(t)/\epsilon$.
We thus conclude 
\begin{equation} \label{eqn:ratio-bound}
\Econd{q(t)/p(t)}{q(t)} \le \min \paren{\alpha q(t)/(\alpha q(t) - \hat{\epsilon}) ,\ q(t)/\epsilon}\mbox{.}
\end{equation}
Setting $q(t) = (\hat{\epsilon}/\alpha + \epsilon)$ to maximize this
quantity yields an unconditional bound of 


$\E{q(t)/p(t)} \le 1 + \hat{\epsilon}/\alpha\epsilon$.


To bound $\E{q(t)}$ in terms of $\E{p(t)}$, note that for all $q$
\begin{align*}
q/\Econd{p(t)}{q(t)=q} & \le \Econd{q(t)/p(t)}{q(t)=q}\\
                    & \le 1 + \hat{\epsilon}/\alpha\epsilon
\end{align*}
where the first line is by Jensen's inequality, and the second is by 
equation~\ref{eqn:ratio-bound}.
Thus $q \le \paren{1 +
  \hat{\epsilon}/\alpha\epsilon}\Econd{p(t)}{q(t)=q}$ for all $q$.
Taking the expectation with respect to $q$ then proves 
$\E{q_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)} \le \paren{1 +
  \frac{\hat{\epsilon}}{\alpha\epsilon}} \E{p_{\ensuremath{v}}(t)}$
as claimed.
\end{proof}
